explanation: Traverse the BST in reverse inorder: right subtree, node, left subtree. This visits keys in nonincreasing order, so stop as soon as k values have been collected. Recursive calls carry the shared result list and stop once its size reaches k.
timeComplexity: O(h + k) time for height h. The initial descent is at most h edges, followed by at most k emitted nodes and their traversal work.
spaceComplexity: O(h) auxiliary space, plus O(k) output space. The traversal keeps at most height-sized pending nodes and a k-element result.
attribution: Unmodified reference source: epi_judge_cpp_solutions/k_largest_values_in_bst.cc. Elements of Programming Interviews Judge authors; repository LICENSE: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International. Explanation authored for EPI Practice.
correctness: Reverse inorder visits every right-subtree key before its root and then its left-subtree keys, so BST values appear in nonincreasing order. Stopping after k visits therefore returns exactly the k largest keys.
walkthrough: For [7,3,11,1,5,9,13], reverse inorder begins 13,11,9,7. With k=3, stop after [13,11,9]. The walkthroughCase uses the judge’s JSON input format and expected observation.
edgeCases: Stop before traversing unnecessary smaller subtrees.
k=0 returns an empty result when supplied.
Preserve repeated keys if the EPI BST input permits them.
